chapter: Wagon bands, halls and the old brass bands
title: Irish and Black longshoremen: rivals who respected a fair fight
summary: Danny describes Irish and Black dockworkers competing for hard work and settling disputes by fighting.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: They had a thing going. All the element of people, the poor oppressed Irishmen come here, starving from the potato famine, they settle in New Orleans. You have the Negro here. They're both working. They're rivals for the hardest work, uneducated work in town. But they have a common thing in one another. They were still longshoremen. So you don't say nothin' about these Nigger longshoremen and you don't say nothin' about them Irish longshoremen. They come over there and...

Yeah. They (?) hard work. Don't talk. Put up or shut up. Make it. And they'd work together. They use different toilets, just so they got so (?), and then they let them all use the same toilet. They respected one another, and they wanted to know if you was a man.
Many times they had fights on the river where a White longshoreman made a remark to a Black longshoreman, and they said, "Well, go out and settle it out on the (?)." And

they'd go out at twelve o'clock, and the two (?) would get out there and fight. And all of them would sit around, the Black and White, and look, and the best man wins. We ain't talkin' about no goddamn color now. Just fight. You're a man, I'm a man. So many times that's been on the river(?).
